catalog_quote: Ik must be viewed as a ‘tone language’ because in Ik “the pitch of a word can change the meaning of the word. Not just its nuances, but its core meaning” (Yip 2002:1). ... As a lexical tone language, Ik falls in the company of all the neighboring Surmic languages like Didinga, Eastern Nilotic languages like Teso-Turkana, Western Nilotic languages like Acholi and Lango, and Southern Nilotic languages like Pokot and Kupsabiny. But Ik differs from nearby ‘tonal accent’ languages like East Cushitic Dhaasanac that allow only one high tone per word (Tosco 2001:34). And from within the Kuliak group, Carlin “found no evidence of So being a tone language” but rather that “stress-accent is important in So, not on the paradigmatic level, but rather on the syntagmatic level” (1993:16). ... Unlike pitch or tonal accent languages, Ik exhibits a wide range of lexical tone patterns or ‘melodies’. These…

new_statements.quote: Ik is a tonal language, but because the tone system has yet to be adequately analyzed, it will not be dealt with here. A basic analysis of Ik tone is forthcoming. Nevertheless, an effort has been to mark lexical tone in the data. High tone is marked with an accent aigu, low tone with an accent grave, and mid tone is left unmarked.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's 'tonal' coding from Schrock 2014 (ch. 3 sec. 3.2): the 2011 sketch already calls Ik 'a tonal language' and marks three lexical tone levels, but offers no stress statement and no tone analysis, so it neither refines nor contradicts the 2014 grammar (which supersedes it, cf. Schrock 2014:28 'a phonological sketch (2011b)').
new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper classes Ik as a tonal language with lexical tone (transcribed as High / Mid / Low with acute, unmarked, grave), explicitly defers the analysis of tone to later work, and says nothing at all about word stress or accent: the words 'stress' and (prosodic) 'accent' do not occur in the 40 pages; sections cover vowels, consonants, and syllable types only.
new_statements.exceptions: none; only the tentative remark that high tone correlates with vowel lengthening (p. 35)
new_statements.identity_note: Ik (Icé-tód) as spoken by consultants from villages in Timu Forest, Kaabong District, northeast Uganda (data: 1,700-word list collected 2008).

tone_statements.citation: Schrock, Terrill B. 2015. A Guide to the Developing Orthography of Icetod. Lokinene, Uganda: Terrill B. Schrock. 122 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 61499; issue date 2015-03; PDF '', 569 KB).
tone_statements.quote: Icetod has been analyzed as having two basic tones: High (H) and Low (L). But these two tones get pronounced in several other ways depending on the lexical or grammatical context they appear in. One could say, then, that at a psychological level, Icetod has two ‘tones’, but at the level of pronunciation it has several other pitch types—level pitches and falling or rising pitches. ... each syllable (rhythmic vowel or vowel-consonant combination) gets its own tone designation. So, a word with three syllables gets three tones, one with four syllables gets four tones, and so on.
tone_statements.locator: p. 47, ch. 3 Tone, intro; after '..' p. 48, sec. 3.1 Tone on words
tone_statements.summary: Two underlying tones H/L, one per syllable; surface high, high-falling (depressor consonants), mid (hidden/floating H), mid-rising, low; floating H in optative; minimal pairs given; nothing on stress.

audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal' (tonal-OR-pitch accent, domain not stated by the source) rests on the best available description: a 747-pp 2014 reference grammar with a full tone chapter, held held by the project, cross-checked against the same author's 2017 LangSci sketch, also. Every fragment of the deciding quotation was re-verified verbatim at the stated printed pages (2014 pp. 99, 100, 103, 124; 2017 p. 489). The grammar explicitly calls Ik a lexical tone language, explicitly distinguishes it from pitch/tonal-accent languages (no limit on H tones per word), contrasts it with stress-accent So, and nowhere states a word-stress rule; the only prosodic hedge (possible syllable-weight/tone interaction, 'rules yet to be discovered') is already captured in the record's domain_quote.
